content: 1. The telehealth assessment was widely regarded as a valuable tool by all stakeholders. It was seen as a means to enhance the quality of service delivery and improve broader health outcomes. 2. In the Netherlands, a service delivery system included domestic and car adaptations based on medical assessments for 318 adults with spinal cord injuries. While satisfaction with the availability of services was acceptable, satisfaction with the service delivery procedures was notably low. Satisfaction with available services was significantly related to adherence to wheelchair provision guidelines. 3. In Italy, a study involving 79 powered wheelchair users evaluated the effectiveness of a nine-step protocol for wheelchair service and provision. The outcomes were generally positive, with significant economic benefits, including reduced social costs. 4. In Croatia, wheelchair services provided to 104 members of the Croatian Paraplegic and Tetraplegic Alliance included wheelchair assessments and selection processes. Satisfaction with wheelchair dimensions and comfort allowed participants to engage more in daily activities and feel safer. However, many participants were excluded from parts of the process, negatively impacting their daily living activities, safety, and satisfaction with the wheelchair and services. 5. In the USA, the Honolulu Wheelchair Seating Clinic provided oneto two-hour assessments by physical therapists for 26 clients. While clients were satisfied with the clinic and therapists, they noted a need for improvement in follow-up on equipment orders and fittings. 6. In the Philippines, two paraplegic patients participated in a 30-minute telerehabilitation session. The session reduced expenses, eliminated travel fatigue, and lessened the burden on families. Perceived benefits included no early wake-ups, no waiting in clinic lines, and direct communication with doctors. 7. In Indonesia, a study compared 118 users receiving services based on the WHO 8-Step model with 24 users receiving standard care. Data collected at baseline and follow-up (3-6 months) showed that training did not significantly improve long-term wheelchair skills. 8. In Ireland, wheelchair services were described as ad-hoc and non-uniform, with limited access to assessments, follow-ups, repairs, and education. Participants reported reduced independence due to barriers in the wheelchair provision process. 9. In Zimbabwe, 55 wheelchair users participated in a project based on WHO guidelines. Statistically significant improvements in satisfaction with wheelchair features, service delivery, and function were observed, except for adult satisfaction with follow-up and child satisfaction with training. 10. In Kenya and the Philippines, wheelchair users identified challenges in repairing and maintaining wheelchairs, dissatisfaction with services, and a need for family training. The study highlighted the importance of addressing these issues to improve service outcomes. 11. A review of wheelchair services revealed that they often failed to meet all user needs. Issues included long waiting times, poor maintenance, strict eligibility criteria, and differing opinions on needs. There was a consensus that services were doing their best, but improvements were necessary. 12. Telehealth wheelchair assessments were found to reduce travel time and costs for both users and health professionals. However, some remote specialists expressed concerns about the process. 13. In a study on satisfaction with wheelchair services, more than half of adult users reported being quite to very satisfied with their recent services. However, there were areas for improvement, particularly in follow-up and maintenance procedures.
